item.title: Energy Brief: Saudi Aramco Cuts Europe Off From October Crude as Macron Seeks Emergency Stock Release; Record Diesel and TTF Prices Push G7 Toward Action
item.description:
Saudi Aramco told European term buyers they will receive no crude in October after the East-West pipeline outage, rerouting roughly 60 million barrels through Hormuz to Asian refiners instead. With Europe's diesel benchmark above $200 a barrel, Macron is calling the G7 back to the table for another emergency stock release while EU gas storage sits at two-decade lows.
► Saudi Arabia Cuts Europe to Zero on October Crude as Pipeline Workaround Skips the Continent Saudi Aramco has told European term customers they will receive no Saudi crude in October, with at least two European refiners informed their October allocations are zero and people familiar with the decision saying it applies to all European term bu Why it matters: The geographic split in Saudi export recovery is stark: Asia gets the crude that once bypassed Hormuz, while Europe — whose refiners relied on the Yanbu-SUMED route — is cut off entirely. It reveals how a chokepoint war reorders who gets energy, with the Atlantic basin losing access even as Gulf oil flows partially resume.
► Macron Calls for Another Emergency Oil Release as Europe's Diesel Crisis Deepens French President Emmanuel Macron said Friday he will convene G7 countries in the coming weeks to coordinate stock levels, exports and production capacity and consider tapping strategic reserves, as Europe loses Saudi crude and diesel prices push deep Why it matters: Europe is being forced to burn its strategic stockpile on products, not just crude, and the G7 has largely exhausted the stock-release lever. The shift signals that the continent is now managing an acute end-use fuel crunch — diesel and jet fuel — that pipeline repairs, stock releases and alternate crude sourcing cannot quickly solve.
► Oil Heads for Weekly Loss as Saudi Export Fears Ease, but Benchmarks Stay Elevated Oil prices were set for a weekly decline after three weeks of gains as fears that Saudi Arabia could not keep exporting eased on reports of the ship-to-ship transfers, Reuters and OilPrice. com report. On Friday, Brent traded around $103. Why it matters: The weekly fall shows the market's worst-case supply fears have been priced back, but the relief is partial — oil still holds above $100 and the physical premium (Dated Brent near $130) is far steeper than the futures curve suggests, because rerouting Gulf barrels to Asia has not helped the Atlantic basin.
► LNG Cargoes Begin Pushing Through Hormuz as Qatar and UAE Test the Chokepoint At least two LNG carriers have transited the Strait of Hormuz this week, while two others were detected in ship-to-ship transfers offshore Oman, according to tanker-tracking and satellite data compiled by Bloomberg. Why it matters: The restart of LNG transit through Hormuz — even in trickles — is the first real sign Gulf gas producers are adapting to the blockade using the same STS playbook oil has used. But volumes remain a fraction of pre-war, and the winter competition between Europe and Asia for non-Hormuz cargoes keeps prices structurally tight.
► Germany Confronts a Record-Low Gas Storage Crunch With Just Weeks Before Winter Germany, Europe's biggest economy and the owner of the world's fourth-largest gas storage capacity, is weighing an expanded market incentive to lift storage levels after sites stood only 56% full in mid-September — the lowest in at least a decade and Why it matters: Germany's storage shortfall is the EU's single biggest winter risk — the country alone holds a quarter of the bloc's capacity. Its move to pay traders to refill rather than buy gas directly, as in 2022, is a market-based adaptation to an energy security emergency, but 56% full with weeks to go leaves little margin against a cold spell.

item.title: Energy Brief: Trump Claims Direct Talks With Iran as War 'Hopefully' Nears End; UN Panel Flags US War Crimes in Iran
item.description:
President Trump says he has spoken to Tehran 'directly' and that Iran 'wants to make a deal,' teeing up a UN General Assembly push with Gulf leaders next week. Separately, a UN fact-finding mission found 'reasonable grounds' the US committed war crimes in two Iran strikes, even as oil slid to a one-week low on Saudi reroutes.
► Trump Claims Direct Talks With Iran Ahead of UN General Assembly Push President Donald Trump told reporters Wednesday he has spoken to Tehran 'directly' and that the Iranians 'want to make a deal,' declaring the war, which began on Feb. 28, is 'hopefully' nearing its end, Fox News reports. Why it matters: A real or perceived channel to Tehran — however fragile — repositions the US-Iran conflict a week before UNGA, where a face-to-face or leader-level contact could test whether the 'wants to make a deal' line holds beyond rhetoric. It also gives Trump a domestic off-ramp ahead of midterms focused on gas prices.
► UN Panel Finds 'Reasonable Grounds' of US War Crimes in Iran A UN fact-finding mission said Thursday it found 'reasonable grounds' to believe US forces committed war crimes in two airstrikes in Iran, and that Iran committed crimes against humanity, AP and Bloomberg report. Why it matters: The war-crimes finding gives critics and neutral capitals documentation to attach to the US campaign right as Trump seeks a negotiated exit, complicating the messaging of a deal and feeding domestic and international pressure over the conduct of the conflict.
► Oil Slides to One-Week Low as Saudi Arabia Reroutes Exports Through Oman Oil prices fell to a one-week low Thursday, with Brent settling at $104. 82 (down 1%) and WTI at $101. 91, after reports that Saudi Arabia was moving crude through Oman to offset its damaged east-west pipeline, Reuters and Fox News report. Why it matters: Saudi rerouting via Oman partly cushions the pipeline outage, but it also signals the kingdom is pushing more barrels through Hormuz — the very chokepoint Iran claims to control — tying Saudi supply security more tightly to US naval protection and to the fate of the diplomacy.
► US Approves $24.3 Billion F-35 Sale to Saudi Arabia The US State Department approved the sale of 48 F-35 stealth fighter jets to Saudi Arabia in a deal worth $24. 3 billion, announced Thursday, Reuters and the Financial Times report. Why it matters: Approving the F-35 to Riyadh — during an active war with Iran — signals the US sees Saudi Arabia as its enduring regional security anchor regardless of how the Iran talks resolve, and gives Riyadh leverage it can use against Houthi and Iranian pressure on its energy infrastructure.
► ExxonMobil Nears Orinoco Return as the US Rush Into Venezuela Deepens US supermajor ExxonMobil is nearing a preliminary deal to invest in Venezuela's oil fields, with talks focused on the Petromonagas project in the Orinoco Belt, Mother Jones and World Energy News report. Why it matters: The rapid succession of deals — Chevron, then Continental/Hamm, now ExxonMobil — shows Washington's Venezuela pivot is consolidating quickly, pulling US majors into the world's largest reserves, and squeezing Chinese operators out of Orinoco assets as Caracas trades access for revenue under US military threat.
► LNG Price Surge Prices Out Asian Buyers, While Europe Faces a Lean Winter Asia is set for its weakest September LNG imports in eight years as high spot prices deter buyers in China and South Asia, while Europe keeps paying up, Reuters reports across two analyses. Why it matters: The crunch is being exported to Asia even as Europe 'is saved' — a reminder that the LNG market's pain is borne by price-sensitive emerging buyers in China and South Asia, reshaping who can afford energy in a war-driven supply squeeze with no obvious relief in sight.

item.title: Energy Brief: Continental Strikes Venezuela Orinoco Deal as Trump's Sanctions Pivot Takes Shape; Iraq Pushes OPEC for 6M bpd Baseline
item.description:
Oklahoma shale giant Continental Resources and investor Heeney Capital signed Venezuela deals Wednesday, marking the clearest move yet by US firms into the sanctioned country's energy sector. Separately, Iraq is pressing OPEC+ to raise its baseline to 6 million bpd citing reconstruction needs, while Brent slid below $105 as the Saudi East-West pipeline repair race dominates the market.
► Continental Resources, Heeney Capital Sign Venezuela Deals in Test of Trump's Sanctions Pivot Oklahoma-based Continental Resources signed a memorandum of understanding with Venezuela's state oil company PDVSA on Wednesday to operate and develop the Ayacucho 2 Block in the Orinoco Belt — a 126,000-acre area holding an estimated 30 billion barr Why it matters: This is the concrete, deal-level translation of a policy shift that had been mostly rhetoric: Washington is moving from sanctioning Venezuela's energy sector to brokering US corporate entry into it.
► Oil Slides Below $105 as Middle East Disruptions Ease, Saudi Pipeline Repair Race Looms Brent crude fell $1. 25, or 1. 22%, to $104. 62 a barrel while West Texas Intermediate declined $1. 16, or 1. 2%, to $101. Why it matters: The price is caught between two forces: headline-driven relief on the diplomatic/military side, and a hardening physical shortage as Saudi export capacity stays impaired. The East-West pipeline is the escape valve that lets the kingdom bypass the choked Red Sea and Hormuz routes — if it stays down, the slide below $105 could reverse quickly.
► Iraq Asks OPEC+ for a 6 Million bpd Baseline, Citing $400B Reconstruction Needs Iraq is seeking a 6 million bpd OPEC+ production baseline, up from its current 4. 431 million bpd, as Baghdad pursues an aggressive expansion of its oil industry despite severe export disruptions, Bloomberg reported and Yahoo Finance echoed. Why it matters: Iraq's demand lands at a delicate moment: OPEC+ is trying to stabilize prices near $100-plus while members eye how much they can pump once export routes reopen. If Iraq gets anywhere near a 6 million bpd baseline, it reshapes the alliance's spare-capacity math for years.
► OPEC Output Fell 900,000 bpd in August; Saudi Arabia Down to 6.98 Million bpd OPEC crude output dropped 900,000 barrels per day in August, with Saudi Arabia's production falling over 1 million bpd to 6. 98 million bpd amid the chokepoint disruptions, according to cryptobriefing's tracking of OPEC data. Why it matters: This quantifies the war's real supply damage at the producer level: the kingdom is pumping at levels far below its installed capacity because it cannot ship. It underscores why the East-West pipeline repair is not just a market story but a national-output story, and why Iraq's quota ambitions look abstract while actual production is bottlenecked.
► Europe Spends Record €7.3bn on Russian Arctic Gas in Eight Months as Winter Squeeze Builds Europe has spent a record €7. 3 billion on Russian Arctic LNG in just eight months, surpassing the entire 2025 total, per an MSN review of trade data. Why it matters: The Yamal figure exposes a stubborn contradiction in Europe's energy posture: states sanction Russian oil while their utilities and shipping firms keep Arctic LNG flowing into the continent.
► Russia and Ukraine Press On With Energy Strikes Despite Trump Ceasefire Claims Ukraine reportedly struck the Yaroslavl oil refinery in western Russia — drones entered the industrial zone and footage appeared to show the facility on fire after explosions — while Russia hit petrol stations in Kyiv, according to Yahoo News and the Why it matters: The pattern is unchanged: whatever is said at the diplomatic level, neither side is treating energy infrastructure as off-limits. The continued refinery strikes keep Russia's domestic fuel supply under pressure and sustain the crude-flow re-routing story that has been reshaping...

item.title: Energy Brief: Saudi Warns It Will Respond Firmly as Houthi Red Sea Blockade Draws Riyadh-Cairo Alliance; Oil Holds Near $107 as Hormuz Diplomacy Stalls
item.description:
Riyadh escalates its confrontation with the Houthis over control of the Bab el-Mandeb while Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman travels to Cairo for security backing. Simultaneously, the planned Iran-Oman Hormuz shipping talks are postponed and the tanker El Gaia becomes the flashpoint in a US-Iran blame war over who hit it — keeping Brent above $107.
► Saudi Arabia Vows 'Firm' Response as Houthi Maritime Blockade Tightens on the Red Sea Saudi Arabia on Tuesday warned it would react 'firmly' to Yemen's Houthi rebels after a series of ballistic missile and drone attacks wounded 13 civilians in the kingdom's south, according to The Hindu's live coverage of the West Asia war. Why it matters: With Hormuz still choked by the US-Iran war, the Houthi grip on Bab el-Mandeb closes off Saudi Arabia's alternative export route. The kingdom is now fighting a two-front energy war — and its Red Sea port of Yanbu, the escape valve for east-west pipeline flows, is directly in the firing line.
► Riyadh-Cairo Summit: MBS Seeks Egypt's Backing for Red Sea Security Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman visited Cairo and met President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi for security talks after 13 people were injured by drone and missile attacks, the FT reported. Why it matters: Egypt is the quiet heavyweight in this conflict — its canal revenue collapse makes Cairo a vested stakeholder in reopening the Red Sea, and Riyadh is seeking an Arab-state front behind its campaign rather than acting alone. A coordinated Saudi-Egyptian posture on maritime security would reshape the regional response to the Houthi blockade.
► Hormuz Diplomacy Stalls: Iran-Oman Talks Postponed, El Gaia Becomes the Flashpoint Oman's foreign minister said the planned meeting between Iran and several Gulf nations on creating a temporary shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz has been postponed, a setback reported by Reuters and the Associated Press. Why it matters: The postponed talks mean the shipping corridor that Gulf states and Iran had been circling remains unfilled, keeping Hormuz transit risk elevated.
► Oil Holds Near $107 as Hormuz Delay and Houthi Attacks Lift Prices Oil prices rose more than 3% on Monday as further Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, strikes affecting shipping around the Strait of Hormuz and the postponement of regional talks increased concerns about Middle East supply disruption, per Yahoo Finance. Why it matters: The market is now pricing in a prolonged, two-route supply problem rather than a single chokepoint. With the East-West pipeline down and Bab el-Mandeb contested on top of the Hormuz disruption, Saudi Arabia's ability to serve both its customer bases is structurally impaired — and the price reflects that there is no quick diplomatic fix in sight.
► IEA and OPEC Both Slash Demand Outlooks as the War Bites The International Energy Agency, in its September report, slashed its 2026 global oil demand forecast to a 2. Why it matters: The war is now destroying demand faster than it is destroying supply — a dynamic that complicates price expectations. Even with severe supply losses, the demand-wipeout story means the market may not spiral as high as supply alone suggests, and both IEA and OPEC are signalling the economic pain of $100-plus crude is already suppressing consumption.
► Europe Braces for a Costly Winter: UK Bills Seen Jumping 25% Bloomberg Economics forecasts UK household energy bills will jump by about 25% in January as the Iran war drives up wholesale gas and electricity prices, adding to inflationary pressure. Why it matters: The war's inflation shock is now moving from oil markets into household bills in Europe and Asia. item.title: Energy Brief: Oil Slides Toward $90 as US-Iran Pause Holds for Third Night; Iran Says It Controls Hormuz, Won't Seek Talks
item.description:
A US-Iran pause on strikes has held for a third night, sending oil prices plunging 7-9% after Monday's spike above $108, even as Tehran insists it controls the Strait of Hormuz and is not seeking talks. The market is pricing a diplomatic off-ramp that Iran's rhetoric has yet to confirm.
► Oil Crashes as US-Iran Diplomatic Pause Holds The sharpest oil-market reversal in weeks played out as the US and Iran paused strikes for a third consecutive night while mediators report progress on a diplomatic opening, per today's reporting. Why it matters: The violent round-trip reveals a market dominated by headline diplomacy, not physical barrels. Any collapse of the pause will re-spike prices faster than the slide down.
► Iran Says It Controls Hormuz, Won't Seek Talks — Contradicting Pause Narrative The diplomatic picture is muddier than the market's rally suggests. Why it matters: When Iran's official line and Washington's read diverge this openly, the 'progress' mediators cite may amount to little more than an agreed silence. The market may be over-discounting re-escalation risk.
► Saudi Pipeline Stays Dark as Iraqi Drones and Houthis Keep Targeting Oil Sites Saudi Arabia's East-West Petroline — its only pipeline bypassing Hormuz — remains shut after Iraq-origin drones destroyed the line on September 10, a strike that also sent US diesel to a record with no backup route, per MSN reporting. Why it matters: The dual chokepoint pressure — Hormuz contested and the Petroline bypass destroyed — is structural supply damage that a diplomatic pause does not repair. Even a 'deal' leaves Saudi export capacity crippled for months.
► US Uses Snapback to Block Iran's Nuclear Chief From IAEA Meeting Washington escalated the nuclear dimension of the standoff by blocking Iran's nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami from attending the IAEA General Conference in Vienna, using the UN snapback mechanism to deny him entry, according to Reuters and Khaleej Time Why it matters: Banning Iran's nuclear chief from the IAEA is a deliberate hardening signal that undercuts the softer 'pause' narrative — it tells Tehran that Washington intends to keep maximum pressure on the nuclear file even while probing de-escalation on the military track.
► BRICS Summit Delivers United Front Against the US War — With Energy Backdrop Leaders of emerging powers including Russia and Iran projected a united front at Modi's New Delhi BRICS summit, issuing a joint statement targeting the US-launched war in the Middle East and Washington's sanctions, BusinessMirror reported. Why it matters: The BRICS joint statement formalizes an anti-Western energy-trade bloc at the same moment India becomes Russia's critical fuel supplier. Russia's war-driven dependency on Indian refined products is cementing a trade architecture Washington's sanctions cannot easily sever.
► Critical Minerals: US Invests, But China Still Grips the Chain A new report from the REEII (published via Reuters, Sept 14) finds that despite US government initiatives, China remains dominant in the supply of critical minerals crucial for clean energy. Why it matters: For all the strategic-rhetoric around 'de-risking,' the REEII finding is a blunt reality check: Western investment is flowing, but China still controls the midstream processing that determines who actually wins the critical-minerals contest.
■ The Bottom Line Energy markets spent the day swinging violently on the US-Iran pause — oil plunging 7-9% and sliding toward $90 after Monday's spike above $108 — but the rally rests on diplomacy that Tehran publicly rejects. Iran says it controls Hormuz and won't seek talks even as Trump claims Iran wants a deal, while the Saudi Petroline bypass stays dark with ~7 million bpd shut in and Washington simultaneously hardens the nuclear track by barring Iran's nuclear chief from the IAEA. item.title: Energy Brief: Russia's Fuel Imports From India Hit Record as Refinery Strikes Redraw Crude Flows; Trump Urges Halt on Diesel Attacks
item.description:
Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries forced Moscow to import a record 172,000 tonnes of oil products in August, 70 percent of it from India, even as Trump publicly urged Kyiv to stop targeting Russian diesel. Meanwhile Brent pushed toward $108 after satellite images confirmed heavy damage to Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline.
► Russia's Record Fuel Imports From India Expose a Circular Crude Economy Russia imported a record 172,000 tonnes of oil products in August, more than seven times the previous monthly record and three times its total imports for all of 2025, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), reported by H Why it matters: Ukraine's drone campaign has effectively erased Russia's status as a refiner-exporter, forcing Moscow into a costly, sanctions-laden re-import loop while its product export revenues hit their lowest since the 2022 invasion.
► Trump Urges Kyiv to Stand Down on Russian Diesel Strikes US President Donald Trump called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday to halt strikes on Russian diesel infrastructure, blaming the attacks for driving fuel shortages, according to multiple reports including Seeking Alpha, Daily Times Why it matters: The request signals rising US pressure to treat Russian refineries as a global fuel market issue rather than purely a military target, potentially constraining Kyiv's most effective tool for draining Russian export revenues.
► Saudi East-West Pipeline Damage Worse Than Acknowledged; Yanbu Stocks at 5-7 Days Satellite images released Sunday night show a pumping station on Saudi Arabia's 1,200 km East-West pipeline charred and badly damaged after Friday's drone attacks, the Guardian reported, citing Vantor imagery. Why it matters: The outage removes Saudi Arabia's principal escape valve from the Hormuz disruption just as Houthi advances tighten control of Bab el-Mandeb — collapsing both of the global oil system's main alternate routes simultaneously.
► Hormuz Diplomacy Stumbles as Oman Postpones Iran-Gulf Meeting Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, announced late Sunday that a planned Monday meeting between Iran and Gulf Arab states was postponed 'in the interests of consensus', the Guardian, Reuters, Bloomberg and the New York Times reported. Why it matters: The postponement dashes near-term hopes for a quick reopening of the world's most critical oil chokepoint, keeping roughly 20 percent of global seaborne crude at risk and underpinning the price spike.
► Brent Pushes Toward $108 as Red Sea, Black Sea and Hormuz Strains Converge Brent crude rose more than 3. 4 percent to $108 per barrel on Sunday, a level not seen since May, the Guardian reported, as the market digested the Saudi pipeline damage on top of the stalled Hormuz talks. Why it matters: Three of the world's critical energy arteries — Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb and the Black Sea export corridor — are simultaneously degraded or closed, producing a supply shock that OPEC's lowered demand outlook cannot offset near term.
► India's Rising Role as the Arbitrage Centre of a Fractured Oil Market Beyond the Russian fuel trade, India is emerging as the key arbitrage node in a market where sanctions and war have scrambled normal trade routes. Why it matters: The war is entrenching a circular India-Russia energy relationship that sanctions architecture has not closed — refining Russian crude into products Russian consumers need, then shipping them back under layered circumvention.
■ The Bottom Line For the second day running, the dominant energy story is a supply-side shock: satellite-confirmed damage to Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline leaves Yanbu weeks from running dry, simultaneously knocking out Saudi Arabia's Hormuz bypass just as Oman postponed the Iran-Gulf shipping talks and Houthis tighten their grip on Bab el-Mandeb. item.title: Energy Brief: Iran Nears Hormuz Shipping Deal With Oman; Gulf States Set Salalah Summit as IAEA Sends Tehran to UN Security Council
item.description:
Tehran says a temporary safe-route agreement for the Strait of Hormuz is days away and Gulf foreign ministers will meet Iran in Oman on Monday, even as the IAEA board referred Iran's nuclear file to the UN Security Council for the first time in two decades — two tracks that will shape the next phase of the crisis.
► Iran Says Hormuz Shipping Deal With Oman Is Days Away Iran said a deal with Oman establishing a temporary safe shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz is 'days away,' according to Bloomberg and Reuters reporting cited across outlets. Why it matters: This is the first concrete diplomatic instrument proposed to reopen Hormuz, but it is not neutral — it would institutionalize Iran's role as gatekeeper of the world's most important oil artery, with Tehran collecting fees on movement.
► Gulf States and Iran to Meet in Salalah on Monday Foreign ministers from Gulf states, alongside representatives from Iraq, will meet Iran on Monday, September 14, in Salalah, Oman to discuss maritime security and navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, regional officials said. Why it matters: Gulf states opening direct maritime-security talks with Iran, days after the US sank Iranian tankers and bombed the country, reveals a widening gap between Gulf capitals and Washington's approach.
► IAEA Sends Iran's Nuclear File to UN Security Council for First Time in 20 Years The IAEA Board of Governors voted 23-3 to refer Iran's nuclear file to the UN Security Council, a step not taken in two decades, on a resolution backed by Western nations citing nuclear 'non-compliance,' Reuters and IAEA reporting show. Why it matters: Escalating Iran's file to the UN Security Council while the country's enrichment sites lie in ruins is diplomatically significant but practically limited — there is little left to 'divert' and no inspection regime to restore while the war is active.
► Europe Heads Into Winter With Gas Storage at a Near Two-Decade Low European gas storage is at its lowest level for this time of year in nearly two decades, with the EU entering the heating season about 15 years' low by some measures, per reporting from outlets citing EU data and the Wall Street Journal. Why it matters: With Qatari supply interrupted and Asia outbidding Europe for cargoes, European storage — already depleted heading into autumn — leaves the continent exposed to a brutally expensive winter. The gas picture is now the clearest channel through which the Hormuz war is translating into a cost-of-living shock across Europe, independent of crude prices.
► India Turns to Russia for Critical Minerals as Modi-Putin Talks Deepen During recent Modi-Putin discussions, India signaled it is looking to Russia to plug gaps in critical minerals and rare earths, seeking greater control over sourcing, processing, and value addition, according to regional reporting on the talks. Why it matters: India leaning on Russia for critical minerals and rare earths deepens Moscow's role as a commodities anchor for the non-Western world, mirroring the oil relationship that has kept Russian crude flowing to India despite sanctions.
► Markets: Brent Near $104 as Supply Crunch and Diplomacy Pull Both Ways Brent traded near $104. 6 with WTI around $100. 1 and Gulf-grade Murban at a wide premium near $119. 5, reflecting the steep repricing of Gulf crude specifically, per OilPrice. com price data. Why it matters: The market is oscillating between two opposing forces: a supply crunch that has producers refusing to hedge and forecasters raising price calls, and the prospect that a Gulf-Iran navigation deal could start loosening the strait.

item.title: Energy Brief: Saudi Shuts East-West Pipeline After Iraq-Launched Drone Strike; IEA Cuts 2026 Supply Outlook Again
item.description:
Saudi Arabia suspended its East-West export pipeline — the kingdom's main bypass around a blocked Strait of Hormuz — after drones launched from Iraq hit pumping infrastructure, while the IEA cut another 1.4 million bpd from its 2026 supply outlook and pushed Gulf flow recovery into 2027.
► Saudi Arabia Shuts East-West Pipeline After Iraq-Launched Drone Attack Saudi Arabia suspended operations on its East-West crude pipeline — the artery that reroutes roughly 5 million bpd toward Yanbu on the Red Sea, bypassing a stricken Strait of Hormuz — after it was hit by drones launched from Iraq. Why it matters: This is the first confirmed shutdown of Saudi Arabia's principal Hormuz bypass route, targeting the infrastructure Riyadh has leaned on since the strait closed. The pipeline carries roughly a third of Saudi export capacity and repairs, even to pumping stations, take time — a direct hit on the kingdom's remaining export channel.
► Riyadh's Restraint Marks a Shift in Gulf Diplomacy Equally notable is what Saudi Arabia did not do. Why it matters: Saudi choosing not to strike back at Iraq — even on a pipeline it depends on — signals Riyadh is managing escalation carefully while at war across multiple fronts. But it also invites the question of how many more hits the kingdom's infrastructure can absorb before restraint becomes unsustainable.
► IEA Slashes 2026 Supply Outlook Again, Pushes Gulf Recovery to 2027 The International Energy Agency cut another 1. 4 million bpd from its 2026 global oil supply outlook in a report released Friday, now seeing output fall 5. 7 million bpd (~6%) this year versus the 4. Why it matters: The IEA is now effectively modeling a deep, sustained supply shock, not a temporary disruption — and it is simultaneously cutting supply and demand forecasts, acknowledging a shortage severe enough to destroy consumption. That divergence with OPEC reflects genuinely different reads on whether this is a demand-led or supply-led contraction.
► Hormuz Traffic in Single Digits as Houthis Take the Whole Red Sea Coast Ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz slumped to single digits Thursday — just seven vessels in 24 hours, two outbound and five inbound, versus a 10-day average of 15 — per Kpler data cited by Reuters and OilPrice. com. Why it matters: The twin chokepoints — Hormuz throttled and Bab el-Mandeb now effectively hostile — together explain why Saudi's East-West pipeline matters so much: it is the only major artery still connecting Saudi export volumes to open water, and it was just struck.
► The Refining Crunch: White House Eyes Defense Production Act as Diesel Tops $6 The White House is considering using the Defense Production Act to add U. S. refining capacity, with American refineries running at 98% utilization and U. S. diesel prices above $6 per gallon for the first time, Reuters reported. Why it matters: The war has exposed that the world's bottleneck is no longer just crude molecules, but the ability to turn them into diesel and other fuels. Using a Cold War-era defense tool to expand refining capacity signals the shortage has moved from market problem to national-security problem in Washington's view.
► China Restocks: Imports Hold at 7.2 Million Bpd as Buying Recovers China is on track to import about 7. 2 million bpd of crude in September, roughly flat with August and extending a recovery from June's decade-low of 7. 1 million bpd, per Kpler tracking cited by Nikkei Asia and OilPrice. com. August imports rose 6. Why it matters: China's re-entry is the clearest signal yet that the world's largest importer judges this supply shock as survivable at current prices — either because it has enough reserves to buy opportunistically, or because alternative, non-Middle-East supply is proving workable.

item.title: Energy Brief: Houthis Capture Mocha in Push on Bab el-Mandeb as Saudi Output Hits 36-Year Low; Putin Brings Energy to Delhi BRICS
item.description:
Iran-backed Houthis seized the Red Sea port of Mocha and Zuqar Island, advancing on Bab el-Mandeb, while data showed Saudi crude output plunged to its lowest since 1990. Putin's arrival in New Delhi for the BRICS summit puts energy and critical minerals at the center of India-Russia talks.
► Houthis Seize Mocha, Open a Second Front on Bab el-Mandeb Iran-backed Houthi forces captured the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha on Thursday, with a Yemeni military source telling AFP the rebels were advancing toward the Bab el-Mandeb strait 'after having taken control of Mocha. Why it matters: This is a new theater in the chokepoint war: having tightened its grip on Hormuz traffic, Tehran's proxies are now working to replicate that squeeze at Bab el-Mandeb — the Red Sea outlet that Saudi Arabia has been diverting crude through since its Hormuz route was shut.
► Saudi Output Slumps to 36-Year Low as Both Export Routes Are Cut Saudi Arabia reported to OPEC that its August crude output fell by 1. 9 million bpd to 6. 238 million bpd — the kingdom's lowest production since 1990 — while exports plunged to 3. Why it matters: OPEC's de facto leader has lost access to both its primary export chokepoints simultaneously — an unprecedented bind that is removing spare capacity from the market while prices are already above $100.
► Putin Lands in Delhi for BRICS as Energy and Minerals Top the Agenda Russian President Vladimir Putin touched down in New Delhi on Friday for the BRICS summit, his first overseas trip in this phase of the war, with bilateral talks with PM Modi scheduled on the sidelines, per Times of India. Why it matters: As Western energy ties strain under sanctions, India is deepening a dual-track Russia relationship — discounted crude now, and critical-mineral supply chains for its green transition — at a moment when oil at $100-plus makes the economics of that discount far more attractive to Delhi.
► US Moves on Kenya Minerals as Rare Earth Stocks Slide on Sino-US Thaw Hopes The United States, through assistant secretary of state for Africa Frank Garcia, said it will help Kenya build mineral-processing factories, with one report pegging the proposed package at about $62 billion (8 trillion Kenyan shillings), focused on t Why it matters: Washington is simultaneously courting new processing partners in Africa and betting on diplomatic de-escalation with Beijing — two strategies whose market signals are pulling in opposite directions.
► OPEC Cuts 2026 Demand Outlook for Fifth Straight Month OPEC downgraded its 2026 oil demand growth forecast by 200,000 bpd to 380,000 bpd, leaving total consumption at 105. item.title: Energy Brief: UAE Severs All Trade With Iran After Missiles Fall Near Its Coast; Hormuz Traffic Slows to Six Vessels as Oil Holds Above $91
item.description:
The UAE formally halted all trade, financial and commercial ties with Iran after two ballistic missiles fell near its coast, a sharp break between two Gulf neighbors that deepens the region's economic fracture. Meanwhile Hormuz tanker traffic slid to six vessels on Tuesday and Brent held above $91 as both Washington and Tehran showed no appetite for talks.
► UAE Freezes All Trade With Iran After Missiles Fall Near Its Coast The United Arab Emirates has halted all trade, financial and commercial ties with Iran until further notice, after saying Tehran fired two ballistic missiles that fell near its territory, OilPrice. com reported Wednesday. Why it matters: The UAE has been one of the Gulf's most pragmatic traders with Iran, and its decision to sever all economic ties is a qualitative break — not just a security posture but a commercial rupture.
► Hormuz Traffic Slows to Six Vessels; Oil Rises for a Fourth Day Commodity vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz slowed further on Tuesday, with ship-tracking data from Kpler showing just six commodity vessels transiting the waterway, down from nine on Monday and below the 10-day average of 11, Reuters repor Why it matters: The market is now pricing a prolonged closure rather than a reversible shock. With transit volumes near a tenth of normal and both sides refusing talks, the question has shifted from when Hormuz reopens to how long the world absorbs the disruption — and whether alternative export routes out of the Gulf of Oman can meaningfully offset the shortfall.
► Saudi Aramco Reroutes September Barrels to Europe via Egypt and Malta Saudi Aramco will supply full contractual crude volumes to at least three European refiners in September, offering deliveries from Egypt, Saudi Arabia and through ship-to-ship transfers off Malta as the war disrupts the kingdom's normal export routes Why it matters: Saudi Arabia is actively re-engineering its export logistics around two blocked chokepoints — Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb — by routing crude through Egypt and using ship-to-ship transfers.
► Murban Crude Jumps to 4-Month High as ADNOC Cuts Asia Supply The price of Murban crude, the UAE's flagship grade, surged to a four-month high this week, trading at a nearly $7 per barrel premium over Brent at $97. Why it matters: ADNOC's decision to trim spot supply to Asia — even as it expands overall exports — shows the UAE is prioritizing premium pricing over volume in a tight market.

Why it matters: The gap between Washington's two-year promise and the four-year-plus reality highlights how far the region is from a genuine Hormuz alternative.

Why it matters: The war's cost is now hitting household budgets directly — UK bills at a three-year high and inflation rebounding, while India scrambles to shift households off imported LPG onto domestic piped gas.

Why it matters: Ukraine's sustained drone campaign against Russian refining is now visibly constraining Russia's export capacity — diesel exports at multi-year lows even as global markets are tight.
